summary: For ages 7–9, build respect-centred understanding that rainforest indigenous peoples are living experts whose deep ecological knowledge — plants as medicine/food/materials, and shifting cultivation that is sustainable when plots are small and rested long enough — has been built and tested over thousands of years, and that modern science continues to learn from it. Make knowledge concrete with specific ethnobotany examples and treat shifting cultivation as a regenerative cycle contrasted with permanent clearance of nutrient-poor rainforest soil.
misconceptions: 'Indigenous knowledge is just superstition/stories' — it is detailed, empirical and often centuries ahead of documented science.
'All farming destroys rainforest' — small-scale shifting cultivation can be sustainable; scale and permanence are the problem.
'These peoples lived long ago' — they are contemporary communities managing forests today.
'Modern science knows best' — much rainforest medicine and ecology was first known to indigenous peoples.
'Shifting cultivation = slash-and-burn destruction' — conflating small rotational plots with large permanent burning for cattle/soy.

activities.title: Forest pharmacy: plants and their tested uses
steps: Examine a scene showing several rainforest plants, each paired with a traditional use: a slender vine used to stun fish for easy catching, a bark used to ease fever, a fruit tree providing both food and building wood.

For each plant, state its traditional use in your own words. For the fish-stunning vine and the fever bark, read the added note that chemists later studied the very same plant or a substance from it (the vine's fish-stunning substance and the bark's fever medicine); the fruit tree simply shows food and building wood.
Explain aloud why 'the people of the forest knew this first' shows real expertise rather than luck or guesswork.
Give at least two examples of indigenous forest knowledge from memory.
activities.insight: Indigenous ecological knowledge is detailed, empirical expertise — and for several documented plants, modern science later studied and confirmed the same effect — not folklore or stories.

activities.title: The shifting-cultivation cycle vs permanent clearance
steps: Follow a small clearing through its full cycle: a small plot is opened, cropped for a few years, then left to rest while the forest slowly closes back over it.

Beside it, observe a permanently cleared strip, shown in this illustration as bare and cracked, that never regrows into forest and becomes degraded because the nutrient-poor soil is used up and never rested.
Explain in your own words what shifting cultivation is and why it harms the forest less than permanent clearing (the plot is small, is left to regrow, and the soil restores).
Answer the probe: if a shifting-cultivation patch were never left to regrow, would it still be sustainable? Explain why not.
activities.insight: Small-scale, rotational clearing left to regrow for long enough is a sustainable cycle; it is large scale, permanence, or rest periods too short for recovery — not any tree-cutting at all — that destroy rainforest.

activities.title: Operate the cycle: a shifting-cultivation simulation
steps: Choose a plot size and how many years before moving on, then watch soil fertility and forest regrowth respond.
Try a small plot farmed for only a few years before moving on and left to rest for a long time, and observe that in the model the soil restores and forest regrows.
Try a large, permanent plot and observe that fertility collapses and the land stays bare.
State the rule you discovered: small + rotational sustains, large + permanent collapses.
activities.insight: The sustainability of shifting cultivation can be felt as a system: outcomes depend on plot size and whether the land is left to regrow.

activities.title: Learning from the expert: a respectful apprentice dialogue
steps: Take the role of a respectful learner asking a knowledge-holder questions such as 'How do you farm without exhausting the soil?' and 'Which plant would you use for a fever?'
Listen to the expert's spoken answers and ask a follow-up question driven by your own curiosity.
Afterwards, retell two things the expert taught you, using present tense.
Describe how this knowledge and modern science could work together to protect the forest.

Optionally, look at a map of forest peoples and the biodiverse territories they steward, and at an image showing traditional knowledge and lab science converging on a shared goal, to see that these are contemporary communities whose expertise works alongside science today.
activities.insight: Indigenous peoples are contemporary experts; a learner can follow curiosity to understand their expertise and how it complements modern science.

checkQuestion: Indigenous farmers clear a small patch of forest, grow food on it for a few years, then move on and let the forest grow back — this is called shifting cultivation. Is that the same as the deforestation that destroys the rainforest? Tell me yes or no, and then tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: No — it isn't the same. In shifting cultivation the patch is small and is left to regrow, so the forest recovers and the soil restores; it's a sustainable cycle developed over thousands of years. Destructive deforestation clears huge areas permanently (for cattle, soy, palm, logging) and never lets them grow back. Indigenous ecological knowledge — which plants heal, how to farm without exhausting the forest — is real expertise that modern science is still learning from.
